title: How We Decide Which Businesses to Back
excerpt: Whether it's a startup we might build, a client we might advise, or a company we might invest in — the same four tests apply. Here's Alttene's evaluation lens, in the open.
content:
Alttene looks at businesses from three angles: things we might build, clients Alto Partners might advise, and companies we might put money or sweat behind. Different chairs, same lens. Over time that lens has hardened into four tests, and we fail most opportunities on the first one.

Test 1: Is the problem boring and expensive?

The best businesses sit on problems that are unglamorous, recurring, and costly — payroll, logistics, compliance, matching people to opportunity. Boring means underserved by people chasing shiny things. Expensive means the customer already pays for the pain (in money or hours), so you're not inventing a budget line, just redirecting one. If the problem is exciting but optional, the marketing budget will die proving people should care.

Test 2: Does the operator have earned insight?

Not credentials — earned insight: something true about the market that they learned the hard way and most people still disagree with. It usually sounds oddly specific. "Nigerian SMEs will pay for bookkeeping, but only if it lives inside WhatsApp" is earned. "AI will change accounting" is a headline. When we hear the specific kind, we lean forward.

Test 3: Can a small win fund the next one?

We're allergic to plans where nothing works until everything works. The businesses we back have a staircase: a first product a narrow group genuinely pays for, whose revenue and lessons fund step two. Staircases survive bad years. Moonshots need every year to be good.

Test 4: Would we take the founder's call at 11pm?

Sentimental-sounding, but it's risk management. Every business hits a night where the plan is dead and character is the only asset left. Integrity, coachability, and stamina show up in small ways early — how someone handles a missed deadline, a hard question, a term they don't like. We've never regretted walking away from great numbers attached to a person we didn't trust.

What we skip

No scorecards out of a hundred, no fifty-page memos. Four tests, honestly applied, then a decision. The discipline isn't in the framework — it's in refusing to romanticize your way past a failed test because the deck was beautiful.

Building something that passes all four? Our door — and our calendar — is open.
author: Fisayo
